# 【CASE REPORT 】

# Pulmonary Sclerosing Pneumocytoma: A Case Revealed During 8-Year of Follow-up with CT imaging

Mariko Nishihara 1, Ryosuke Imai 2, Takeshi Ushigusa 3, Tomoaki Nakamura 2, Clara So 2, Kohei Okafuji 2, Atsushi Kitamura 2, Fumitsugu Kojima 4, Yutaka Tomishima 2, Torahiko Jinta 2, Naoki Nishimura 2 and Toru Bando 4

## Abstract:

Pulmonary sclerosing pneumocytoma (PSP) is a rare, benign tumor. Given the challenges of a bronchoscopic diagnosis, surgery is performed during the early stages of the disease. Therefore, little is known about the growth pattern of PSP. This case of PSP was not diagnosed despite bronchoscopy, resulting in lung resection eight years after the anomaly was first identified on computed tomography (CT). This report compares the long-term follow-up of CT and pathological findings and discusses the difficulty in making a diagnosis using a bronchoscopic forceps biopsy to aid in future PSP diagnoses and treatment planning.

Key words: Pulmonary sclerosing pneumocytoma, CT imaging, preoperative diagnosis, lung tumor, bronchoscopy

(Intern Med Advance Publication) (DOI: 10.2169/internalmedicine.3956-24)

## Introduction

Pulmonary sclerosing pneumocytoma (PSP) is a rare, benign lung tumor that accounts for 1% of all lung tumors. Originally called sclerosing hemangioma, the current name was determined according to the 2015 WHO classification (1), since PSP is believed to be derived from juvenile type II alveolar epithelial cells. Although PSP is a relatively rare benign lung tumor, it has also been associated with malignant behaviors such as multiple lesions, recurrence, lymph node metastasis, and airway compromise due to its size (2-6). Consequently, distinguishing it preoperatively from carcinoid or adenocarcinoma tumors is challenging (1). Furthermore, pathological diagnosis of PSP using small samples obtained via bronchoscopy is difficult (7). Given its potential malignancy and challenges in the preoperative diagnosis, surgical resection is typically performed at an early stage. Therefore, few reports exist on long-term follow-up of PSP via computed tomography (CT) (8).

We herein report a case of PSP that had been enlarging for eight years and was resected for diagnostic purposes, comparing the CT and pathological findings.

## Case Report

A 52-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented to her physician with pain extending from the left side of her abdomen to her back. Computed tomography (CT) showed a 1.8×1.7-cm nodule in the left lower lobe of her lung. Although bronchoscopy was recommended for the histological diagnosis, the patient opted for regular monitoring via CT. The nodule had increased in size. Considering this, a histological diagnosis was proposed, and the patient was referred to our hospital for further treatment at the time when the tendency of enlargement got to be obvious. During her first visit to our facility, her vital signs, physical examination results, and laboratory test results were normal. On CT with contrast, a 2.5×2.1-cm rounded nodule with small calcifications was noted in the left lower lobe, adjacent to the mediastinum and compressing surrounding bronchi. The contrast effect was gradual and internally heterogeneous in the equilibrium phase. Lymphadenopathy was not observed. The lumen of the peripheral side of B8 and B9+10, which had been preserved eight years ago, was compressed by the tumor (Fig. 1). The tumor had not directly invaded nor did it occupy the bronchial lumen. Instead, the lumen was externally compressed, causing the bronchus lumen to collapse. On fluorodeoxyglucosepositron emission tomography (PET)-CT, the maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax) was 3.51 and 4.03 in the early and delayed images, respectively. Bronchoscopy was performed for the histological diagnosis. Transbronchial aspiration cytology, brushing cytology, and a forceps biopsy with endobronchial ultrasonography were performed to confirm the presence of lesions. Bronchoscopy revealed preservation of the bronchial lumen without tumor invasion. A cytological examination of the Papanicolaou smear revealed the absence of abnormal or atypical cells. Meanwhile, a forceps biopsy revealed peripheral airway tissue with mild atypicality but without obvious benign or malignant findings. The culture test results were negative for both the bacteria and fungi. As the preoperative diagnosis was not definitive, the patient was referred to a thoracic surgeon for diagnostic surgery. Thoracoscopic left lower lobectomy was performed without complications. A 2.3×1.8×1.6-cm, yellowish, well-defined nodule was resected specimen from the left lower lobe, completely separated from the bronchus that it was compressing (Fig. 2-B). Microscopically, the cells were a mixture of round stromal and spindle-shaped cells similar to alveolar epithelial cells, and various structural patterns were noted, including papil-

lary, tubular, and solid patterns (Fig. 3-A, B). Immunohistochemistry was positive for TTF1, Napsin A, EMA, and AE 1/3 (Fig. 3-C, D, and E). No atypia or malignancy was observed. A histopathological examination of the postoperative specimen led to the diagnosis of PSP. She was undergoing annual chest radiography monitoring as part of her medical checkup.

## Discussion

We encountered a 52-year-old woman with PSP who had not been diagnosed preoperatively and underwent surgery for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes after eight years of follow-up. To our knowledge, this is the first case involving long-term CT to compare CT and pathological findings after surgery. PSP is often resected as a diagnostic treatment before long-term follow-up (8) because of the difficulty in preoperatively differentiating it from malignant tumors. Few cases in which the clinical course can be evaluated using imaging have been reported. The most common imaging characteristic at the diagnosis is a solitary, round-to-oval, well-defined nodule (9). However, 1/3 and 1/5 of PSP cases present with indistinct borders and ground-glass opacities outside the tumor, respectively (10). Rare cases of PSP present with multiple nodules, enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes, and distant metastases (11). Several reports with long-term follow-up exist, including cases in which the postoperative lesion did not enlarge in size even after 10 years (12) and wherein the maximum diameter only slightly increased after 6 to 10 years (13-15). In our literature search, most reports of PSP cases with long-term follow-up showed no comparison of postoperative pathological findings with CT findings. In the present case, CT findings showed that the bronchi around the tumor had become enlarged without destroying the surrounding structures (Fig. 2-A). pressed the surrounding bronchial structures without bronchial tissue involvement. These pathological characteristics were consistent with the enlargement patterns observed on CT. These CT findings may help preoperatively diagnose PSP. The accumulation of more cases of PSP will further improve the accuracy of the preoperative diagnosis. In the present case, a preoperative bronchoscopic forceps biopsy did not lead to a definitive diagnosis. In previous reports, the rate of a preoperative diagnosis was as low as approximately 10% (16, 17) because of the generally small volume of specimens that can be obtained by a forceps biopsy. Pathologically, the disease is characterized by two types of cuboidal surface cells and round stromal cells, with two or more of the four different structural patterns of proliferation: papillary, sclerosing, solid, and hemorrhagic (1). A diagnosis requires the pathological confirmation of multiple mixed proliferation patterns. Therefore, collecting sufficient specimens for a diagnosis is difficult, complicating the preoperative diagnosis (18). Furthermore, pathologically, the

tumor cells overlie the normal bronchial epithelium, suggesting that a bronchoscopic forceps biopsy may have difficulty reaching the tumor tissue owing to its anatomical structure (Fig. 2-C). Given the number of specimens and their anatomical characteristics, a bronchoscopic diagnosis is considered difficult. However, case reports have described the preoperative diagnosis of PSP using a cryobiopsy (7) in patients with lesions adjacent to the bronchi, as in this case. Cryobiopsies have been reported to have a higher diagnostic yield than forceps biopsies (19, 20), mainly for lesions adjacent to the bronchus. This may be due to the larger available specimen volume and ability to perform lateral biopsies. In the present case, the tumor was adjacent to the mediastinum, making a cryobiopsy a risky procedure. We decided to proceed with diagnostic surgical resection when a trend toward enlargement became apparent, given that PSP often has a low diagnostic yield in bronchoscopic forceps biopsies. However, in cases in which sufficient specimens can be obtained through cryobiopsy and a pathological preoperative diagnosis is possible, careful follow-up with imaging may be preferable (21).

## Conclusion

We encountered a case of PSP that grew after eight years of CT follow-up and gradually compressed the surrounding bronchi. A pathological examination of the surgical specimen was consistent with the CT findings in terms of the tumor cells proliferation without invading surrounding bronchi. This character may be related to the reason why transbronchial biopsy had yielded inconclusive results for the diagnosis.
